source.title: The Curious Case of Adversarially Robust Models: More Data Can Help, Double Descend, or Hurt Generalization
source.authors: Yi-Fei Min; Lin Chen; Amin Karbasi

record.tranche_reason: The study directly analyzes how test loss changes as training-set size changes, using theoretical and empirical methods on adversarially trained classifiers and regressors. It does not reproduce the original deep-network model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own sample-size sweeps and theoretical results for test loss, recorded below. It also cites prior double-descent results, which are not recorded as rows. The training-set sizes at which rises occur are mostly given symbolically or shown in figures; the paper does not identify them as interpolation thresholds.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own theorems and simulations of test loss on unperturbed data as training-set size grows, for adversarially trained low-dimensional classifiers and regressors. This bears on V3's 'more data can hurt' in a new setting. The rises are driven by adversary strength ε relative to the signal, not by an interpolation threshold. T3 (new setting) fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also conclude that current adversarial training cannot always achieve low error on both perturbed and unperturbed data. They suggest that fundamentally new ideas may be needed, against the tenet that more data helps.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies training-set size for adversarially robust models rather than varying deep-network size or training epochs; it uses theoretical Gaussian-mixture and Manhattan models plus empirical SVM, regression, and Gaussian-mixture experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with adversary strength. The linear-regression threshold also differs by input distribution; the Gaussian and shifted-Poisson thresholds are reported as between 0.6 and 0.8, and between 4.0 and 7.0, respectively. The Gaussian-mixture 0-1 experiments use two tiebreaking methods.

fits_no_version.finding: In adversarially trained low-dimensional models, sample-wise non-monotonicity (help, double descent, or hurt) is governed by ε relative to signal strength μ, not by an interpolation threshold. As ε approaches μ0, the increasing stage becomes arbitrarily long.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-wise 'more data hurts' can arise from adversarial (robust) training at adversary strengths near or above the signal, independent of interpolation.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: Empirical outcomes are presented in figures without numerical test-loss values or reported uncertainty estimates. The paper does not locate the observed sample-size rises relative to an interpolation threshold. The authors describe the Manhattan model as highly simplified and unlikely to model real-world problems.

untested.parts: Whether the rises occur near an interpolation threshold. The models are low-dimensional and never located relative to interpolation; the rises are tied to ε versus signal strength.
All: no capacity sweeps past interpolation.
All: no label-noise or regularization-tuning analysis.

missing.what: Simulated test loss vs n under linear loss (d=1, μ0=1, σ0=2) for weak, medium and strong ε, with standard-model baseline. In the medium regime the error rises faster during the increasing stage as ε grows.
Corollary 2: with equal μ and σ across coordinates, the length of the increasing stage N2(ε)−N1(ε) goes to infinity as ε→μ0 from below.

record.verdict_notes: The paper notes its double descent is sample-wise, unlike Belkin et al.'s parameter-wise curve, and cites Nakkiran et al. for sample-wise double descent. All rows are proofs or synthetic low-dimensional simulations with no error bars; the Manhattan model is explicitly unrealistic. This is one of the original sources' companion settings only by analogy: neither original source is this paper, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweeps in deep networks and the peak's relation to fitting the training set.
Whether the increases occur near an interpolation threshold.
Capacity sweeps across model classes past an interpolation point.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise or variance causation, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Recounting complexity by effective parameter number and testing whether that turns the curve into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.condition: Medium- and strong-adversary regimes (ε near or above the signal strength) in Gaussian-mixture, Manhattan, SVM and 1-D linear regression settings
relationships.reason: Expected unperturbed test loss rises with n over a range (medium) or for all large n (strong), proven and simulated (R2, R3, R5, R7, R8, R10, R11, R13, R15, R17). The mechanism is adversarial strength, not an interpolation threshold.
relationships.display_finding: Expected unperturbed test loss rose over a sample-size interval for medium adversaries and for all sufficiently large sample sizes for strong adversaries, driven by adversarial strength.

statements.correction: Gaussian linear loss: monotonic decrease under Theorem 1(a). Manhattan model: zero loss under Theorem 4(a). Gaussian 0-1 loss: decrease after n = 3 for sufficiently small ε. SVM and regression: decreasing loss in reported weak regimes. Harmful sample increases occur in stronger regimes; interpolation-threshold location untested.
statements.problem: The empirical Gaussian 0-1 loss decrease is qualified as occurring after n = 3. Weak-adversary results without an identified interpolation threshold do not establish a scope limitation of V3 as written.
